[]` on line 17 covers only a missing `questions` key, not a non-array value or a missing field on an element. verifications.suggestedPatch:
Wire the parser to the project, then layer the type-checked tier:

  // eslint.config.js
     ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  +  ...tseslint.configs.recommendedTypeChecked.map((c) => ({ ...c, files: ['**/*.{ts,tsx}'] })),
     {
       files: ['**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
       languageOptions: {
         ecmaVersion: 2022,
         globals: { ...globals.browser },
  +      parserOptions: { projectService: true, tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname },
       },
  ...
  +  { files: ['**/*.js'], ...tseslint.configs.disableTypeChecked },

Risk: this is not a switch flip and should not be sold as one. It will surface a batch of new errors that must be triaged before CI is green again (`no-floating-promises` on the many `void promise` call sites, `restrict-template-expressions`, and `no-unsafe-*` at summarize.ts:52/73, migrate.ts:58, ProfileView.tsx:117, googleBooks.ts:12), and `eslint .` gets materially slower. Land the config and the triage in one branch, or add the tier as `warn` first.

verifications.verifierNote: Both halves confirmed, and I found extra evidence that makes the live-defect half stronger than stated. STRUCTURAL half: src/app/AppShell.tsx:47-56 is verbatim as quoted — a two-arm `if` over `aiError.kind` narrowing an 8-member union (errors.ts:1-9) with no exhaustiveness guard, so a ninth kind falls through silently. LIVE-DEFECT half: errors.ts:53-61 orders `lower.includes('quota')`, then `lower.includes('safety') || lower.includes('blocked')`, and only reaches `statusOf(error)` in the trailing `else` (lines 57-61) — so any message containing 'blocked' preempts the 403 check. I verified the message really does contain it: @google/genai's `throwErrorIfNotOK` (node_modules/@google/genai/dist/vertex_internal/index.js:2941-2967) sets `errorMessage = JSON.stringify(errorBody)` and throws `new ApiError({ message: errorMessage, status })`, i.e. the ENTIRE 403 JSON body lands in `.message`. Google's referrer-restriction body is `{"error":{"code":403,"message":"Requests from referer <...> are blocked.","status":"PERMISSION_DENIED"}}` — 'blocked' is in there, so kind becomes 'safety' and never 'invalid-key'. The strongest corroboration is the repo's own test: errors.test.ts:17 asserts `403 -> 'invalid-key'`, proving that is the intended mapping, while errors.test.ts:29-31 only ever exercises a message containing BOTH 'blocked' and 'SAFETY' — so the collision case is exactly the one the suite does not cover. AppShell:48's re-call of toAiError does short-circuit at errors.ts:46 (`if (error instanceof AiError) return error`) on the already-misclassified error from client.ts, as described. BLAST RADIUS verified by grep across src/: `setShowKeyDialog(true)` appears only at AppShell.tsx:53 and `<ApiKeyDialog>` is mounted only at AppShell.tsx:204; the three consumers are AddBookModal.tsx:83 (via the onAiError prop wired at AppShell.tsx:196), LibraryPage.tsx:80 and LibraryPage.tsx:98 (via useShell()); every other toAiError consumer (BookDetail.tsx:169/189, ChatModal.tsx:72, EReader.tsx:213, QuizModal.tsx:65) only toasts `.message`. One clarification for the report: the minimal fix is in errors.ts:53-61, not at the cited AppShell line — the AppShell change is the structural hardening.

Google returns 403 with 'are blocked.' in the body; client.ts:26 classifies it as 'safety'; AppShell.tsx:49 is false; the key dialog never opens; the user reads 'Gemini blocked this request under its safety filters' with no way to reach the only key-entry surface in the app. This breaks the CLAUDE.md invariant 'Only AI actions gate, and they open the key dialog.'
verifications.blastRadius: 1 narrowing site (AppShell.tsx:49), but it is the sole gateway to the app's only API-key dialog (AppShell.tsx:53 and :204 are the only occurrences in src/). 3 consumers route into it; 5 other toAiError call sites cannot open the dialog at all.

verifications.verifierNote: Every mechanical claim verified — including the load-bearing one about react-router internals — but the impact is a wrong error message, not a failure, so High is a notch too high. CONFIRMED: src/app/routing.test.tsx:94-98 is the suite's only negative-path test and it covers `/book/does-not-exist`, which DOES match `book/:id` (routes.tsx:19) and is redirected by useBookRoute.ts:17-19 — so it exercises the redirect, not the 404. No test in the file visits an unmatched URL. routes.tsx:12-26 declares no catch-all `path: '*'` (read in full). src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx:5-6 is verbatim as quoted: `useRouteError()` returns `unknown` and is narrowed by a lone `error instanceof Error`, with `isRouteErrorResponse` — the library's own tag check — unused. The key claim checks out in node_modules: react-router 8.3.0's `ErrorResponseImpl` is declared `var ErrorResponseImpl = class {` at node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/router/utils.js:787-802, with NO `extends Error` (it merely stores the Error in a `.error` field at line 799 when constructed from one). And the 404 does route to this boundary: router.js:150-154 calls `getShortCircuitMatches(dataRoutes.activeRoutes)` and sets `initialErrors = { [route.id]: error }`, which for a single-root route table resolves to the root route — the one carrying `errorElement: <ErrorBoundary />` at routes.tsx:16. So `error instanceof Error` is provably false and every unmatched URL renders 'Something went wrong / An unexpected error occurred.' WHY MEDIUM: the user-visible outcome is a generic error page instead of a not-found page. No crash, no data loss, no broken flow — the 'Back to library' link at ErrorBoundary.tsx:18-23 still works. Per the spec's scale that is 'erodes confidence... but isn't on a critical path'. It also, like F001, files a test-coverage gap under the severity of the production defect (which lives at ErrorBoundary.tsx:6, not in the test).
verifications.reachability: Fully reachable, low consequence: type or follow any URL with no matching route (e.g. /libary, /settings, a stale deep link) -> react-router raises its internal 404 ErrorResponse -> router.js:150-154 assigns it to the root route -> ErrorBoundary.tsx:6's instanceof check fails -> the generic 'An unexpected error occurred.' renders under 'Something went wrong'. Matters more once the Phase 4 GitHub Pages demo is public and stale links exist.
verifications.blastRadius: 1 narrowing site (ErrorBoundary.tsx:6) plus the missing test. That single `instanceof Error` check is the app's only error-message surface, so it swallows the detail of every non-Error thrown value, not just 404s.
verifications.amendedDescription: The routing suite's only negative-path test (src/app/routing.test.tsx:94-98) covers `/book/does-not-exist`, a URL that DOES match `book/:id` (routes.tsx:19) and is redirected by useBookRoute.ts:17-19. No test ever visits a URL with no matching route, and routes.tsx:12-26 declares no catch-all `path: '*'`, so react-router raises its own 404 and — via getShortCircuitMatches (react-router/dist/development/lib/router/router.js:150-154) — assigns it to the root route's errorElement. src/app/ErrorBoundary.tsx:5-6 receives it from `useRouteError()`, whose declared return type is `unknown`, and narrows with a single `error instanceof Error`. react-router 8.3.0's ErrorResponseImpl (react-router/dist/development/lib/router/utils.js:787) does NOT extend Error, so that branch is never taken and every unmatched URL renders the generic 'An unexpected error occurred.' under 'Something went wrong' instead of a not-found page. This is the permanent-`unknown` pattern: an unknown crossing a boundary, narrowed once, with the residual arm silently swallowed while the library's own tag check, `isRouteErrorResponse`, goes unused. Severity is Medium rather than High: the outcome is a wrong error message on a typo'd or stale URL, not a crash or data loss, and the recovery links still work — but it will be user-visible once the Phase 4 public demo ships.
